articles.title_orig: US Stocks Waver as Election, AI Bubble Risks Weigh on Outlook
articles.title_zh: US Stocks Waver as Election, AI Bubble Risks Weigh on Outlook
articles.content_orig:
Buckle up for another wild week in markets.
Investors are still coming off a roller coaster ride that included a painful sell-off in the AI trade on Friday, but the volatility isn't expected to die down soon, and a handful of potential catalysts is lies ahead for investors.
This week's docket includes more Big Tech earnings , economic data updates, and the midterm elections, which have historically been a hurdle for markets to clear.
And then there's the fragile state of the AI trade, which was rattled last week as concerns about capex and overall AI demand rocked the market. The Nasdaq 100 , which logged its worst month in over a year, is now on the edge of entering an official correction, with the tech-heavy index down 9% from its high in early October.
Here's what investors are facing next:
Apple , the largest company in the world by market cap after Nvidia's plunge last Friday, is on deck to report results for the third quarter after the bell on Monday, a marquee event that's expected to shape sentiment in the tech trade after last week's sell-off. Here's what Wall Street is expecting from the iPhone maker:
Investors will be paying special attention to the firm's comments on AI. Apple isn't a capex story the same way companies like Meta and Microsoft are. Its spending is expected to come in at around $11 billion to $14 billion this year, compared to the $100+ billion from AI hyperscalers, but the market remains eager to see what the iPhone maker's AI ambitions will look like in the post-Tim Cook era. The coming earnings call will be the first to be led by new CEO John Ternus , setting the tone for the tech giant's new chapter.
The market has been mercurial on Big Tech earnings lately, with investors ready to punish big AI firms at any whiff of bad news. Meta and Tesla were negatively impacted after reporting third-quarter results that hinted at slight changes in spending outlooks, triggering fears that slowing investment could spark a wave of knock-on effects for other suppliers in the industry.
Amazon and Alphabet, on the other hand, spooked investors by suggesting capex would grow next year despite negative cash flow, leading the market to punish those tech giants for what it saw as excessive spending.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
Palantir , another notable player in the AI universe, will also report earnings after the bell.
"We continue to evaluate the monetization versus spending conundrum for hyperscalers," Eric Freedman, the CIO at Northern Trust, wrote in a note on Monday. "While results were very company-specific, the common threads markets focus on are capital expenditure plans, financing needs, existing business cannibalization and evidence of returns."
Oil is an enduring story in markets in 2026, one that's sparked major bouts of volatility in both stocks and bonds. On Monday, Brent and West Texas Intermediate crude eacg dropped 6% as investors took in the possibility that the US and Iran could revive attempts at a diplomatic resolution to the war.
State Secretary Marco Rubio said President Donald Trump preferred to wrap up the conflict with Iran "peacefully," adding that the president hasn't yet decided to attack Iran.
However, more volatility could be looming.
Oil prices spiked in recent weeks on a New York Times report that the US and Israel are drawing up plans to strike Iran after the midterm elections. Energy markets could see more volatility this week if the market sees fresh signs evidence that peace talks are progressing or the administration signals that strikes will resume.
After months of anticipation, the midterm elections are finally here.
Wall Street is eyeing the passing of the midterm elections as a potential catalyst for markets. Stocks have historically struggled into the midterms, but have seen strong gains in the months following, with the S&P 500 gaining an average of 14% in the six months after the midterms since 1970, according to an analysis from BlackRock.
JPMorgan Private Bank said it was eyeing "outsized" gains in the S&P 500 , pointing to improved market breadth, or the measure of winning stocks to losing stocks, in the overall index lately. The bank also recently lifted its year-end price target for the S&P 500 to 8,000, implying 4% upside from the index's current levels.
The bank's market intelligence team flagged near-term volatility depending on the results of the election and outlined the possible reaction in stocks depending on each election outcome.
S&P 500 drops as much as 25 basis points or gains as much as 50 basis points.
Some investors fear an "AI sell-off" in the event of a Democratic sweep, but in that scenario, any pullback in markets would be an "opportunity to buy the dip," strategists wrote in a note.
"SPX has been up a year after every midterm election since 1950 with an average gain of around 15%," the bank's Craig Cohen wrote in a client note. "I suspect that at least part of the reason for this tendency is that the midterms tend to see the incumbent party loses seats and gridlock in Washington tends to be good for Wall Street."
" Volatility could stay up awaiting results. Typically, stocks rally after midterms, but one exception was 2018—also a rate hike year," Joe Mazzola, a head trading and derivatives strategist at Charles Schwab, wrote in a note.
Finally, investors will get a major macroeconomic update in the October jobs report on Friday. It's a data point that could shape the Fed's projected path for interest rate hikes through the rest of this year and early next year.
Central bankers left rates unchanged at their last policy meeting , as expected, pointing to the need to assess the trajectory of inflation before moving rates further. Markets, though, are expecting a rate hike at the Fed's next policy meeting, with the probability of a 25 basis-point rate increase rising to 78% on Monday, according to CME FedWatch.
A strong jobs report, while good news for the economy, risks creating a reason for investors to sell stocks. The logic is that a stronger job market reflects the economy's capacity to absorb higher interest rates, a possible drag for risk assets.
Economists are expecting the US to have added 55,000 payrolls last month, up from the 29,000 jobs added in September.

articles.title_orig: Apple Launches Beta Versions of Watch AI Listening Tools, New Health App
articles.title_zh: Apple Launches Beta Versions of Watch AI Listening Tools, New Health App
articles.content_orig:
The watchOS 27.3 beta adds Live Rewind and Siri Recap to the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4.
The watchOS 27.3 beta adds Live Rewind and Siri Recap to the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4.
It’s impossible to paint a full picture of what Audio Intelligence on the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 will be right now. The watchOS 27.3 developer beta just dropped earlier this afternoon, and these features are meant to be lived with in day-to-day life. We’re definitely going to do that over the next few weeks at The Verge . That said, here are some initial impressions.
What’s newly available today is Live Rewind and Siri Recap. The former lets you see a transcript of the last 15 seconds, while the latter provides high-level summaries of your conversations. (The other two Audio Intelligence features have been available for the last few weeks. I wrote about those in my Series 12 review .) And as always, this is the developer beta. These features could still change quite a bit before a final version arrives for the public.
The first thing I noticed is that these features are not turned on by default. I wasn’t expecting anything different, but it’s worth remembering that these features don’t automatically turn every Apple Watch into a surveillance device. Audio Intelligence requires the latest Apple Watch hardware, a compatible version of iOS (so in this case, the iOS 27.3 developer beta), and someone has to actively choose to enable these features. You can download the beta and double-press the crown to initiate a Live Rewind. It won’t do anything. You must opt in via your iPhone’s Watch app. Same goes for Siri Recap. Enabling Live Rewind also requires an initial microphone calibration with your phone.
Privacy-wise, Apple has publicly available support documentation about its approach to these features. I’m not weighing in on how well it executes them in this hands-on. But Apple has pretty clear messaging in the onboarding process. There are quite a few customization options for when Siri Recap is active. You can get pretty granular. For example, you can have Siri Recap only on at the office during weekdays from 1 PM to 4 PM if that’s when you have meetings. This is hard to convey to bystanders, and I think ethical use should come with an in-person heads-up to the people you frequently interact with. (Hello, fellow Verge writers and editors.)
Live Rewind, so far, has worked as described — with the heavy caveat that I’ve only tested it in my quiet home office with my spouse. Even so, it takes a hot second to learn the timing of a double press. My spouse noticed the audible chime signaling the feature is in use, though they didn’t notice the animation. I’ll have to see how this fares in louder environments. Siri accurately captured our attempts to get my cat to roll over, though in subsequent tests, it misheard a word or two.
I’m more hesitant to comment on Siri Recap. It’s not just because I haven’t had an organic, lengthy spoken conversation yet since downloading the beta. (Siri did not deem my brief conversation with my spouse as worthy enough for recapping.) But I won’t really get a feel for how this feature feels until I’ve tested it in a wide variety of scenarios. Will it work if I talk to myself aloud? How well does it filter out gossip? How will this change how people speak to me? That’ll be the true test of this feature and Apple’s bystander privacy claims. I’ll keep testing and will add an update once I’ve finally received my first Siri Recap.
What I will say is that I’ve been testing the Amazon Bee Frontier for the past few weeks. In the little time I’ve spent with the watchOS 27.3 beta, the differences between Audio Intelligence and the Bee are very clear. The latter has more of what I’d call an AI-forward presence. Bee, for example, offers insights about the emotional tone of a conversation. I’ve also found that the AI can be a bit judgy about insights and takeaways. Live Rewind is just a straight transcript. Again, I’m still waiting on my first Siri Recap, but what Apple’s said publicly so far is that these are meant to be highly factual notes to jog a person’s memory. And, as far as I can tell, there is no commerce angle for Siri Recaps, whereas Bee has an Amazon integration that surfaces buying suggestions based on conversations.
In any case, I’ll be diving deep into these features in the days to come. Let us know in the comments what you’re most curious about.

articles.title_orig: Beijing launches diplomatic flurry amid threat of renewed U.S. war with Iran
articles.title_zh: Beijing launches diplomatic flurry amid threat of renewed U.S. war with Iran
articles.content_orig:
Beijing launches diplomatic salvo to woo Gulf leaders and bolster its influence in the region
China has held a flurry of meetings with Gulf leaders in a sign that Beijing is stepping up its diplomatic efforts in the Middle East.
The diplomatic salvo comes before a highly anticipated meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping when the US president is expected to attend the Apec conference in Shenzhen, China, on 18 and 19 November.
Xi held talks with Haitham bin Tariq , Oman’s sultan, in a historic state visit to Beijing on Monday.
President Xi’s foreign minister, Wang Yi, met Saudi Arabia’s national security adviser, Musaad bin Mohammed Al Aiban, and the deputy secretary of Iran’s national security council, Ali Bagheri Kani.
Haitham’s trip to Beijing is the first time that an Omani head of state has visited China since the two countries established diplomatic relations nearly 50 years ago. According to a Chinese readout of the meeting, Xi warned that the Middle East should not become an arena for “great power rivalry and geopolitical conflicts”.
He said: “China has always been actively committed to stopping conflict and promoting peace, and hopes to contribute wisdom and solutions to resolving the regional security dilemma.”
Wang said after his separate talks that China was willing to “play a constructive role in helping the region emerge from the shadow of the pandemic and achieve lasting peace and stability”. In his meeting with Bagheri Kani, Wang said China supported Iran “in safeguarding its sovereignty and security”. According to China, the Iranian official said his country looked forward to China “playing a more important role in international and regional peace”.
When the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran in February, China was credited with pushing Tehran toward ceasefire talks in Pakistan , bolstering its status as a regional mediator.
Beijing’s influence in the Middle East is “no longer what it used to be”, said Shen Dingli, a Shanghai-based scholar of international relations. But he added: “Given China’s increased investment and trade in the region … its influence cannot be ignored.”
As the war has dragged on, China’s diplomatic efforts have been muted. Its biggest economic leverage over Iran is the fact that it buys about 90% of the Middle Eastern country’s crude oil exports. Between April and June, it slashed its crude imports by 30%, with the total in June plunging to the lowest level in a decade. That saved the global economy from a major spike in inflation. According to some estimates, China’s cut in oil imports shaved $30 or more off barrel prices of Brent crude, a global benchmark.
Beijing has otherwise done little to broker peace in the Middle East. That is partly because it does not see the conflict as being its responsibility to resolve. In March, Wang said the war “should never have happened” and that the US and Israel would find “no popular support” for the strikes.
China is also a beneficiary from the damage that the fighting has done to the US’s global reputation.
According to findings published in July by the Pew Research Center, a Washington-based thinktank, China is now viewed more favourably than the US in a majority of 36 countries surveyed.
The pain caused by the long-term disruption to the strait of Hormuz, the waterway through which much of the world’s oil and gas flows, also poses a risk to China’s economy. Shortages of energy cause inflation, which risks reducing global demand for Chinese goods.
Tehran and Washington are locked in intensive talks to reach an agreement, which could include reopening the strait. Trump has repeatedly threatened to renew military action against Iran after Tuesday’s midterm elections in the US, a move which would cause alarm in Beijing.
Trump’s desperation to reach a deal in the Middle East may also provide an opportunity for China to present itself as a regional peacemaker, bolstering Xi’s status before their meeting. Beijing brokered a detente between Saudi Arabia and Iran in 2023 but since then its diplomatic impact in the region has been limited.
Shen said China’s desire to improve diplomatic relations with Middle Eastern countries as well as the US were “mutually reinforcing” trends.
China’s foreign ministry spokesperson, Mao Ning, said on Monday that China would send special envoy Zhai Jun to Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia in early to mid-November.

articles.title_orig: Apple announces Fitness+ Gym Strength program with personalized workout plans
articles.title_zh: Apple announces Fitness+ Gym Strength program with personalized workout plans
articles.content_orig:
Apple wants to help you get stronger. Apple Fitness+ is expanding to the gym with a new strength training experience. Gym Strength is now available in beta, bringing personalized workout plans, exercise demonstrations, and Apple Watch logging to your lifting routine.
Gym Strength creates progressive, four-week plans based on your strength goals, experience, schedule, and available equipment. After you complete each week of workouts, the following week adapts based on the reps and weight you logged.
The feature is designed for a range of experience levels, from people trying strength training for the first time to experienced lifters looking to make progress. It also aims to help anyone who wants to build a more consistent routine.
When building a plan, you choose your workout days and the body areas you want to focus on. You can select five exercises per workout, which Apple estimates will take about 20–30 minutes, or seven exercises for about 45–60 minutes, depending on your pace.
Each workout recommends exercises, reps, sets, and how much weight to lift.
You move through the workout at your own pace, with short video demonstrations from Apple Fitness+ trainers available for each exercise. The demonstrations can be expanded to show the movement from three different angles.
Apple says Gym Strength includes over 350 exercises across more than 30 types of strength training equipment, including dumbbells, kettlebells, suspension trainers, cable machines, and barbells. Dumbbells are the minimum equipment requirement.
Plans account for the equipment available to you, so the experience can work in a commercial gym or a home gym.
If a machine is occupied or you’re training somewhere with different equipment, you can swap equipment or choose an alternative exercise with a similar movement and body focus. You can also add sets or skip exercises.
Gym Strength requires an iPhone running iOS 27.3 or an iPad running iPadOS 27.3. An Apple Watch running watchOS 27.3 optionally lets you view exercises and log reps and weight from your wrist, while tracking heart rate and calories burned.
Gym Strength also introduces Training Note, an optional feature powered by Apple Intelligence that previews workouts, explains progression, and highlights milestones. Training Note requires an Apple Intelligence–enabled iPhone or iPad with the device set to English.
Gym Strength is included in the existing Fitness+ subscription. It joins a library of trainer-led workouts spanning 12 workout types, including Strength, HIIT, Yoga, Pilates, Core, Cycling, Rowing, Dance, Kickboxing, treadmill walking and running, and Mindful Cooldown.
Fitness+ also offers guided meditations, personalized recommendations, and Custom Plans for scheduling workouts, with new sessions added every week .
Apple Fitness+ costs $9.99 per month or $79.99 per year in the U.S., and a subscription can be shared with up to five other family members. New subscribers can try one month free, while eligible device purchases include a three-month trial.
Fitness+ is also included in Apple One Premier, which costs $39.95 per month in the U.S. and bundles Apple Music, Apple TV, Apple Arcade, Apple News+, and 2TB of iCloud+ storage.

articles.title_orig: Germany’s Merz warns Europe needs seat at the table as Trump renews Ukraine talks
articles.title_zh: Germany’s Merz warns Europe needs seat at the table as Trump renews Ukraine talks
articles.content_orig:
Speaking alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Berlin on Tuesday, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said he had seen no sign that Russia is serious about negotiating a ceasefire in Ukraine.
Zelenskyy and Merz both said the European Union must help shape any lasting peace.
Germany expects European representatives to be in Abu Dhabi for next week's US-led talks with Ukraine and Russia , though they are unlikely to have a seat at the table.
"It is important that Russia finally and seriously engages in negotiations about a ceasefire and a subsequent peace agreement," Merz said when asked about the Abu Dhabi talks. "I do not see that happening so far."
Zelenskyy said he hopes the Abu Dhabi talks, the first trilateral sit down since February, could pave the way for a direct meeting between the Ukrainian president and Russia's Vladimir Putin, who has thus far refused several offers from Zelenskyy for face-to-face talks.
"We are counting on the fact that work in this format and our other diplomatic steps will open the way to a trilateral format at the level of leaders," he told reporters.
Merz said Europe must have a say on sanctions and postwar security.
He said the local ceasefire in Oleshky could serve as a model for a wider truce, but warned that Russian attacks in the Black Sea risked further escalation. "Russia is precipitating a global food crisis, to the detriment of the poorest nations and countries in the world," he said.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine wanted a halt to attacks on energy infrastructure, safe passage for grain shipments through the Black Sea and further prisoner exchanges.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
The Ukrainian president said a ceasefire alone would not secure a lasting peace. Ukraine would need security guarantees backed by Europe and the US. He insisted Europe must be involved in the negotiations.
"There cannot be a sustainable peace if Europe is not at the negotiating table," Zelenskyy said.
He said Ukraine would join the US, European partners and NATO for talks on security guarantees and reconstruction in Brussels on Wednesday.
The talks in Berlin come as Russia continues to increase airstrikes on Ukrainian civilians.
Zelenskyy said at least 33 people were killed, and more than 50 could be trapped in rubble, after multiple Russian strikes on a school building used as an aid distribution center in the frontline southeastern village of on Monday.
Ukrainian officials said Russian forces launched an initial strike on residents waiting to receive aid, and then hit the same location again after waiting for rescue personnel to arrive on the scene, killing several of them and destroying emergency vehicles.
Speaking in Berlin, Zelenskyy described the strike as "one of the largest Russian killings of this war."
On Tuesday, at least 73 people were injured in a strike on a hospital in the northeastern city of Kharkiv, and 226 patients had to be transferred to other hospitals, regional prosecutors said.
"Ahead of the next winter, air defense and the energy sector are our priorities," Merz said. He said Germany would soon deliver new aid in both areas and provide further winter assistance this year.
Zelenskyy thanked Germany for helping protect Ukraine's skies and supporting its energy infrastructure.
"Without Germany, we would not be as strong as we are," he said.
He said Ukraine urgently needed more air defense equipment, including Patriot interceptors .
Zelenskyy told EU leaders in October that Ukraine would need an additional €70 billion ($78 billion) from European governments next year. Germany plans to host a summit of countries backing Ukraine in mid-November to discuss further support ahead of winter.
The visit coincides with the opening of the two-day Berlin Security Conference, which brings together European officials and defense experts. Russia's war in Ukraine is high on the agenda.
Police said about 3,400 additional officers were deployed for the visit and the conference, with reinforcements from across Germany.
Armed officers guarded barriers around parts of the government district, and special police units deployed snipers. Roads were also closed in western Berlin, including near the Kurfürstendamm shopping avenue.

articles.title_orig: China’s HQ-9B air defense system destroys maneuvering missile in tests
articles.title_zh: China’s HQ-9B air defense system destroys maneuvering missile in tests
articles.content_orig:
Authorities in Beijing announced that the PLA Air Force utilized the HQ-9B surface-to-air missile platform to successfully neutralize targets during a training drill. These objectives consisted of missiles capable of rapid movement and complex maneuvering.
The evaluations of the HQ-9B, a modern addition to the Chinese military inventory, required the interception of two distinct missile varieties. One specific target executed an abrupt mid-air pivot before plummeting toward the earth at extreme velocity.
According to the state media outlet China Central Television (CCTV), the Central Theater Command's Shenwei Missile Battalion within the PLA Air Force carried out the maneuvers.
Personnel from the Shenwei Missile Battalion were not briefed on the specific nature of the incoming threats; they were informed only that the mission involved engaging agile, high-velocity projectiles.
A battalion participant noted that the crew was afforded a mere two-second window to react. In this brief interval, they were required to identify the mysterious object and determine if a launch was necessary.
Military specialist Song Zhongping remarked, in a report by the Global Times , that despite precise radar monitoring, a defense system must possess the capacity for mid-flight trajectory adjustments to successfully follow a target exhibiting erratic flight patterns.
For guidance and tracking during an engagement, the HQ-9B utilizes an active radar homing (ARH) mechanism paired with an inertial navigation system (INS). Beyond its sophisticated steering and engine technologies, the HQ-9B is capable of striking targets that follow non-linear flight paths. Nevertheless, the effectiveness of a missile intercept is contingent upon multiple variables, such as communication reliability, target velocity, reaction speed, and radar precision.
The drill also showcased the PLA's ability to fuse different missile, command, and radar elements into a cohesive air defense web. Expert Song Zhongping clarified that China has established a unified data-sharing architecture for its diverse air defense branches to distribute intelligence on approaching hazards and synchronize their actions. Threats are distributed among various units depending on their proximity and combat readiness.
Hu Yang, another member of the battalion, mentioned that just two minutes elapse between the reception of a high-level warning and the actual interception. While the drill proves the HQ-9B can hit maneuvering missiles, its capacity to stop hypersonic cruise missiles or glide vehicles requires separate validation through authentic combat simulations.
Although the HQ-9B might intercept a target approaching directly, engaging hypersonic cruise missiles or glide vehicles presents an extreme challenge for any surface-to-air hardware. Testing the HQ-9B against maneuvering aerial targets does not verify its effectiveness against operational hypersonic technology. Assessing the system's utility against such weaponry would require distinct trials in practical operational settings.
Earlier, during September 2025, China exhibited numerous air defense assets . Featured hardware included the HQ-29, HQ-19, HQ-9C, and HQ-9B. These platforms represent China's expanding proficiency in defending against diverse missile types and fixed-wing aircraft.
The latest HQ-9B drills highlight the ongoing technical advancement of China's armed forces. Still, the ability of the system to negate sophisticated missile hazards remains unproven until subjected to independent testing in lifelike combat scenarios.

articles.title_orig: Bomb threats on flights, cruise ship cause disruption in Europe, no devices found
articles.title_zh: Bomb threats on flights, cruise ship cause disruption in Europe, no devices found
articles.content_orig:
Seven passenger planes across Europe, two of which departed from the UK, have been inspected following a series of suspected bomb threats.
Two Ryanair flights, one originating from Dublin and the other from Lisbon, were searched after landing in Rome following anonymous tips but no explosives were found, sources at the city's Fiumicino airport told the BBC.
The Dublin flight was escorted by the Italian Air Force until landing. Authorities have also searched planes in Poland, Spain and Bulgaria.
While officially there is no link between them, authorities from various countries will be co-operating to assess whether this was a co-ordinated attack, designed to disrupt airspace.
The UK government described today's incidents as "malicious hoax threats".
In a statement it said it had "one of the most robust aviation security systems in the world, with well-tested processes for dealing with any potential threats, as well as malicious hoax threats, like those we've seen today".
Aviation security expert Paul Mason said bomb threats on passenger planes "don't happen that frequently", which made the latest incidents "unusual".
"It sounds like they've been made in a credible manner across a broad range of airlines," Mason told BBC Radio 5 Live. "That would suggest to me that it's been a very deliberate act by a typical actor rather than a load of coincidental, malicious calls."
He said "there are a lot of processes" that the onboard crew and people on the ground must go through "to validate the credibility of the threat".
A flight may be asked to divert if the credibility of a threat "is of a certain level", Mason added, and in some cases the onboard crew may not even be advised on what the ground operators were dealing with.
In Rome, sources at Fiumicino airport told the BBC police bomb disposal experts carried out standard security protocols to ensure the safety of all passengers and crew.
Inspections of the passengers, luggage, and the aircraft yielded negative results, and the alert has since been cleared.
One plane which landed in Murcia, southern Spain - a Ryanair flight coming from Manchester - was also found not to have any explosives on board, Spanish authorities said.
One passenger later said she was unaware of the bomb threat until after the plane landed.
"We weren't told anything during the flight," Sarah told BBC Radio 5 Live. "The plane stopped quite suddenly and then we were kept on the runway for around 30 minutes."
"Then the fire engines turned up, the bomb squad turned up and we were asked to evacuate," she continues.
Sarah said the plane had not been on the ground a minute before it was "surrounded by fire engines and police and a bomb squad". All the passengers were then escorted by police, leaving all their belongings.
"We were only later told that it was an actual threat, a bomb threat to the plane itself," she added.
Two flights heading to Warsaw were also affected, including one from London Heathrow.
The Heathrow flight was originally meant to land at the Polish capital's main airport, Chopin, but was diverted instead to the smaller Modlin airport, briefly forcing its closure.
A Scandinavian Airlines flight from Copenhagen to Warsaw-Chopin landed as planned.
Later on Tuesday, Bulgarian Transport Minister Georgi Peev said there were bomb threats against two planes travelling to the country's capital Sofia.
He told the state-owned Bulgarian News Agency (BTA) the flights were from the northern Italian city of Bergamo and Ireland's capital Dublin.
The flights into Sofia were not diverted and no explosives were found when the planes were checked, Peev said.
Bulgaria's border police said in a statement sent to the BBC that at around 10:35 (08:35 GMT) it had received an email about "the presence of an improvised explosive device on a flight returning from Bergamo".
"Standard procedures for such incidents were immediately activated, and an operational headquarters comprising representatives of various institutions was convened," the statement said.
The border police added that the same email also reported a "similar threat against aircraft arriving from Dublin".
In a separate development, a bomb alert triggered the evacuation of 1,537 passengers and crew from an Israel-bound cruise ship in Greece, media reports from both countries say.
Initial checks of the Panama-flagged Crown Iris vessel currently docked at a port on the Aegean island of Syros found no explosives, they said citing the Greek Coast Guard. A second inspection is expected shortly.
Tuesday's aircraft incidents come a day after a Wizz Air flight from London Luton made an emergency landing in Budapest, escorted by a Hungarian fighter jet, after a bomb threat.
Wizz Air said later that security checks had been made and nothing was found.
BBC Verify has consulted aviation safety experts about what happens on board a plane when a bomb threat is issued.
Marco Chan, a former pilot for Cathay Pacific Airways and Hong Kong Airlines who is now a senior lecturer in aviation operations at Kingston University, said a bomb threat is considered "genuine until it is resolved, even though most turn out to be hoaxes".
Chan said crews will "quietly search" toilets, galleys and storage areas and will not touch a suspicious item unless it has to be taken to an area on the aircraft designated as the least risky bomb location.
The aircraft's captain will have multiple factors to assess, according to former airline pilot Terry Tozer, an aviation safety commentator.
He said these include what facilities are available at the airport they are being diverted to and how the plane can continue onwards should it turn out to be a false threat.
Chan added that once on the ground, the plane is generally "taken to an isolated stand, passengers are disembarked, and police and bomb disposal teams search it".
Additional reporting by Thomas Copeland, BBC Verify

articles.title_orig: Ukraine's rescuers deal with grim aftermath of aid shelter bombings as Moscow pounds energy targets
articles.title_zh: Ukraine's rescuers deal with grim aftermath of aid shelter bombings as Moscow pounds energy targets
articles.content_orig:
Dozens of people were killed when Russia dropped at least nine bombs on a school building in southeastern Ukraine where they had taken shelter, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Tuesday, describing it as “one of the deadliest attacks of this war.”
At least 33 people have been confirmed dead and another 50 are still unaccounted for after the attack on the building in Komyshuvakha in the Zaporizhzhia region, which local governor Mykhailo Semikin said was being used as a shelter and a humanitarian aid distribution center.
Semikin said they were in a newly-built, EU-funded reinforced basement designed to withstand most strikes, but the massive force of the bombs caused the concrete structure to collapse and a fire broke out.
The shelter was built last year in an effort to keep classes going during wartime, but many civilians have since left as the fighting got closer to the village, and it is not currently used as a school. Instead, local authorities are using it as an administrative center and humanitarian hub.
Masha’s husband was fighting on the front line. But she was the one killed by a Russian drone
The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine highlighted in a statement on Tuesday that the attack took place just as civilians from the area gathered to receive humanitarian aid.
“The timing and location of the humanitarian distribution was well publicized,” said Danielle Bell, the head of the mission.
“Either the Russian armed forces knew that there was a humanitarian distribution taking place, or they failed to take the most basic steps to find out what was happening in this village they were planning to attack. In either case, this attack seems to have violated the most fundamental principles of international humanitarian law.”
Zelensky said the attack came just before Russia launched another massive barrage of hundreds of drones and dozens of powerful cruise and ballistic missiles targeting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure – despite US President Donald Trump’s repeated calls for energy ceasefire .
Ukraine’s Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal said three drones were directed at a substation that is crucial for the operation of the Khmelnytskyi Nuclear Power Plant. He posted to Telegram saying actions like that threaten the nuclear safety of all of Europe, and that Ukraine has informed the UN nuclear watchdog, the IAEA.
“It is very telling that all of this is happening on the day of the US congressional elections. The Russians believe that America will not notice this signal from them. But such terror must be noticed and stopped,” Zelensky said on Tuesday morning.
“Ukraine must be helped to defend its skies, otherwise Russia will never stop its missile strikes. It is essential to help build peace honestly and reliably, and America can do that,” Zelensky added.
The latest attacks by Russia come amid a renewed push for negotiations by the Trump administration. US envoy Steve Witkoff recently held a meeting with Zelensky in Norway before flying to St. Petersburg to meet with the Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Separately, first lady Melania Trump helped to secure a ceasefire in the occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, which enabled the evacuation of hundreds of civilians over the weekend. Trump’s office announced on Tuesday that the first lady would bring together representatives from Russia and Ukraine at the White House on Thursday, calling it “an extraordinary moment in American history.”
A Russian bomb attack killed at least 33 people in a Ukrainian village close to the frontline in the Zaporizhzhia region yesterday. CNN’s Clare Sebastian reports.
The strike on Monday is among the deadliest since the start of the war, but the past few months have been exceptionally bloody for Ukrainian civilians.
Russia ramped up its aerial attacks on towns and cities across the country over the summer, striking at all times of the day.
At least 33 people were killed last month when Russia hit two civilian buses in Kramatorsk in the Donetsk region. In August, 38 people were killed when a Russian drone strike on an ammunition depot near the capital triggered a large fire and multiple explosions that lasted hours in a residential area near Kyiv. And a mass Russian missile attack on Kyiv in July killed 33 people across the city in a coordinated barrage.
The assault against Komyshuvakha on Monday followed a familiar scenario in which Russian forces launch the first wave of strikes, wait for emergency services to arrive and then strike again.
At least two first responders, named locally as Denys Konovalenko and Oleksiy Sushchevsky, both 44, were killed after rushing to the scene of the first strike.
The Ukrainian Police said at least four of its officers have also been killed in the attack. They were named as Mykhailo Buzhenko and Mykola Balanda, both of who had more than two decades of police service under their belts, and Mykhailo Romanov and Dmytro Besedin, both of whom have been community police officers for more than a decade.
“(They) were helping local residents take shelter in an underground school. A treacherous follow-up strike trapped everyone who was trying to escape,” the police said in a statement.
Semikin told Ukraine’s national TV broadcast on Tuesday that Russia used KAB-500 and FAB-3000 bombs in the attack.
“To put this into perspective, this is a three-ton aerial bomb containing nearly 1.5 tons of explosive material; such weapons are primarily designed to destroy heavy concrete fortifications and bunkers,” he said.
CNN’s Kit Maher, Victoria Butenko and Clare Sebastian contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Israeli Claims of Iranian Chemical Weapons Divide U.S. Officials
articles.title_zh: Israeli Claims of Iranian Chemical Weapons Divide U.S. Officials
articles.content_orig:
Israel has provided the United States with intelligence indicating that Iran is considering using chemical weapons against its adversaries, but officials in Washington are divided over the information's credibility and significance, The New York Times reported on Tuesday, citing American and regional officials.
Some senior US officials received the intelligence with concern, while others expressed deep skepticism, viewing it as part of a pressure campaign by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government aimed at convincing the Trump administration to resume large-scale fighting against Iran .
According to the report, during discussions with US intelligence agencies and other officials over the past two weeks, senior Israeli officials presented the chemical weapons threat as more urgent than Iran's ambitions to develop nuclear weapons.
Israeli intelligence officials told their American counterparts that they believe Iran is rapidly advancing technology that would allow it to mount chemical weapons on missiles or smuggle them into Israel or another country to carry out an attack.
Other senior American officials believe the threat should be taken seriously, particularly in light of a series of recent warnings about Iranian preparations to attack US interests.
According to the newspaper, there is little disagreement within the American intelligence community that Iran is developing chemical weapons. The central dispute concerns whether Iranian leaders would actually use them, particularly if Iran is not attacked again.
Israel also shared some of the intelligence with officials in Gulf states. Several questioned whether Iran was developing plans to use chemical weapons and believe Israel is attempting to push the United States and its partners toward a more intensive phase of the war.
A regional official told the newspaper that Israel had presented Gulf countries with assessments suggesting Iran was working to make its chemical weapons operational, but had not shared supporting evidence.
According to the official, Gulf governments regarded the claims as lacking seriousness.
For some American officials, the warnings have revived memories of the faulty intelligence surrounding Iraq's weapons of mass destruction in 2002.
At the time, US intelligence agencies presented the White House with a firm assessment that Iraq possessed such weapons, although the country had largely abandoned or suspended its nuclear, chemical and biological weapons programs.
Even among those briefed on the new intelligence, assessments differ regarding how quickly and effectively Iran could deploy chemical weapons.
According to experts and American officials who spoke with the newspaper, mounting a chemical weapon on a ballistic missile is not particularly difficult, but ensuring the effective dispersal of the chemical agent is more complicated.
Smuggling a bomb across a border also presents difficulties. Another possibility mentioned was the use of a drone.
Despite the Israeli warnings, the newspaper reported that preparations for responding to chemical weapons attacks are not a central component of the Home Front Command exercises taking place across Israel this week.
Two Home Front Command officials said there had also been no widespread reminders distributed to officers or the public regarding protective instructions against such a threat.
The IDF declined to comment.
The intelligence was shared as the United States and Iran explore the possibility of a diplomatic breakthrough while simultaneously preparing for a resumption of hostilities.
According to senior American officials, US Central Command (CENTCOM) has a plan for an attack on Iran that could be carried out as early as Wednesday, November 4, one day after the US midterm elections.
The report stated that three American aircraft carriers are currently in the region, while the preferred operational window for an attack is expected to be brief.
One of the aircraft carriers will need to return to its home port after the beginning of November, and particularly dark nights are expected in the coming days, providing favorable conditions for military operations.
However, President Donald Trump has not yet approved a large-scale attack, and diplomatic contacts between Washington and Tehran are continuing.
In recent weeks, the United States has concentrated warships, fighter jets and bombers in the region in preparation for a possible relatively short military campaign involving intensive strikes.
At the same time, diplomats are attempting to formulate an agreement that would reopen the Strait of Hormuz, address Iran's nuclear program and postpone further military action.
According to the report, the military buildup could also serve as leverage to support the diplomatic effort.
Meanwhile, US intelligence agencies assess that the threat to Americans in the Middle East and several other countries is at its highest level since the war began in February.
Intelligence collection was intensified after an Iranian plot to attack a base in Britain used by American fighter jets was uncovered.
On October 23, a warning memorandum regarding potential Iranian attacks was sent to senior administration officials. Diplomats and other personnel were subsequently placed on heightened alert.
The newspaper also linked Netanyahu's efforts to his political situation following the Israeli elections, in which he failed to secure a clear path toward forming a government.
Several commentators who spoke with the newspaper suggested that Netanyahu might attempt to use a national security emergency to pressure opposition leaders into joining a coalition under his leadership.
American allegations regarding an Iranian chemical weapons program date back decades.
In 2003, Iran acknowledged that it had developed chemical capabilities during the Iran-Iraq War but claimed that it subsequently dismantled them.
Tehran denies possessing chemical weapons and has previously described such accusations as psychological warfare conducted by Israel and Netanyahu .
Dana Stroul, a former senior Pentagon official responsible for Middle East policy during the Biden administration, said it has been known for more than two decades that Iran has been stockpiling components for chemical weapons, but has never used them.
However, she warned that Tehran could feel "existential pressure" and potentially cross the threshold into directly using such weapons offensively.
A spokesperson for Netanyahu's office told the NYT : "Israel closely monitors every threat posed by the Iranian terrorist regime and is prepared to confront it."
The White House did not respond to the newspaper's request for comment, but an American official said Trump would defend the United States and its allies against any potential threat.

Oops, something went wrong
Job openings and hiring changed little in September, the Labor Department's monthly Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey showed, as the "low hire, low fire" labor market continued.
There were 7.5 million job openings in September, from a revised 7.2 million a month earlier, the report showed. The hiring rate improved slightly to 3.4%, up from 3.3% in September.
Read more: How jobs, inflation, and the Fed are all related
Layoffs were also little changed at 1.6 million, with 1% of workers losing their jobs. Voluntary quits ticked up slightly to 3.4 million, and the rate of quits rose slightly to 2.1%, from 1.9% in August.
The latest data suggest a continuation of a long labor market trend of slow hiring, but minimal layoffs. A fuller look at the job market will be released on Friday, when the Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes its monthly payrolls report for October. Economists surveyed by Bloomberg expect the US to have added 65,000 jobs last month.

articles.title_orig: Poland launches major border operation as activity in Russia fuels concern over possible "serious provocation"
articles.title_zh: Poland launches major border operation as activity in Russia fuels concern over possible "serious provocation"
articles.content_orig:
Berlin — Poland launched a large-scale security operation this week along its border with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, the country's national police chief said, and the Polish prime minister said the effort may have prevented a sabotage or provocation operation targeting the NATO member.
Additional police and counterterrorism units, as well as troops from the elite military special forces unit GROM, have been deployed as part of the operation, which national police chief Marek Boroń said would run from Monday until at least Nov. 8.
Polish and allied intelligence agencies had warned of possible sabotage operations and provocations during the first half of November, particularly along Poland's border with Kaliningrad, and including possible border incursions by armed groups.
Those warnings had already put domestic security agencies on high alert even before the additional security forces were deployed to the northeast regions of Warmia-Masuria and Podlaskie.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Tuesday that suspicious movements were observed overnight near Kaliningrad, including individuals carrying flashlights close to the border area.
He said the quick reaction by Polish security forces may have prevented an unspecified provocation this week.
"We very quickly mobilized the necessary security forces and means on site, and we successfully prevented any attempted acts of provocation, if that was the intention. Of course, we will never be able to completely confirm that," Tusk said Tuesday, adding that intelligence had pointed for weeks to possible "acts of diversion or more serious provocation" against the European Union, including "the intrusion of armed individuals into Polish territory."
A special command center was set up at Polish national police headquarters to coordinate the new security operation.
The goal is to protect the public, detect suspicious activities early, and prevent attacks on critical infrastructure, the police said Tuesday.
Russia's exclave of Kaliningrad, bordered only by NATO members Poland and Lithuania and the Baltic Sea to the west, is of considerable military and strategic significance. It is widely believed that Russian security agencies, including the FSB and GRU intelligence agencies, have a presence in the territory in eastern Europe.
To the immediate east of Kaliningrad is the strategically important Suwałki Corridor — the only land border connecting the Baltic NATO states with the rest of the alliance, where Poland and Lithuania share a short border sandwiched between Russian and Belarusian territory.
Polish authorities had not published any evidence of specific plans for an act of sabotage or an attack originating from Kaliningrad by Tuesday afternoon, but the alert comes after months of sabotage, air incursion and other low-level incidents across Europe blamed largely on Russia.
During a joint news conference with Lithuania's prime minister on Oct. 13, Tusk referred to a conversation he had recently had with NATO Supreme Allied Commander Alexus Grynkewich, and said it had reinforced his own concerns about increasing threats of sabotage, including possible provocations involving aircraft or attacks on border crossings.
At about the same time, the head of Britain's domestic spy agency MI5, Sir Ken McCallum, painted a dark picture of the security threats facing the U.K. and Europe, and he said that among state threats, "Russia remains aggressor number one."
"The Russian military and intelligence services are once again escalating their attempts at hybrid warfare," McCallum warned, adding that Moscow was "being careful to stay below the NATO Article 5 threshold" with its actions, which would trigger the alliance's collective defense principle .
"It'd be foolish for them to cross" that line, he said, and so far Russia was sticking to "tactics that stop short — though sometimes not much short — of conventional conflict."
Among the numerous incidents attributed to Russia across Europe this year alone, there was a fire in August at a Polish factory that produces drones and other military components, and an arson attack on a Starlink satellite ground station that Polish officials blamed directly on Russia in September.
Russian drones have also crossed into NATO airspace in Eastern Europe repeatedly during the war in Ukraine , and just this week the U.K. Royal Navy said it had intercepted a Russian spy ship off the far northern coast of Scotland.
The navy said helicopters were dispatched to track the intelligence-gathering ship, which was "closely monitoring" a NATO exercise taking place near Scotland's Outer Hebrides islands.

articles.title_orig: Why the Anthropic IPO 'could be the swing vote' for Wall Street bank stocks
articles.title_zh: Why the Anthropic IPO 'could be the swing vote' for Wall Street bank stocks
articles.content_orig:
The midterm elections could reshape Congress as lawmakers grapple with persistent inflation , high energy prices and rising fiscal debt . For investors, by contrast, the political outcome could deliver a boost.
Data from financial firm Edward Jones shows that the S&P 500 stock index rose an average of 1.7% in the month after the last 14 midterm races, dating back to 1970. In the six months following midterm elections, S&P returns averaged 15.5%.
"Volatility around the vote is possible, but markets have historically performed well in the year following midterms as political uncertainty recedes and attention returns to the economic outlook," Magdalena Ocampo, market strategist at the global investment firm Principal Asset Management, said in an email on Tuesday as Americans cast their votes.
With congressional control in the balance, Wall Street analysts are also considering the impact divided government could have on stocks if the Democrats win the House, Senate or both chambers. Political gridlock has historically been good for markets because it limits Congress' ability to pass sweeping tax and spending legislation, reducing the risk of volatility, according to analysts.
"Less change makes a more predictable environment, which allows companies to invest in longer-term projects," Chris Low, chief economist at FHN Financial, a capital markets firm, said in an email Tuesday. "That tends to be good for earnings."
Less stock market volatility doesn't guarantee investors an easy ride, however. Gridlock in Washington, D.C., could also fuel another partisan standoff on the nation's debt, which recently surpassed $40 trillion , or spur the U.S. government to increase its borrowing to fund its priorities, according to economists.
That could unnerve bond investors, who are worried that Washington is on an unsustainable fiscal trajectory, Ed Yardeni, president of Yardeni Research, said in a note to investors.
"Prolonged shutdowns and fiscal standoffs could push Treasury yields higher, weighing on equity valuations," he said.
The Bipartisan Policy Center, a Washington, D.C.-based think tank, estimates that the U.S. will reach the debt limit again sometime between late winter and midsummer of 2027. At that point, lawmakers will have to decide whether to raise the debt ceiling, temporarily suspend it or risk another government shutdown.
Volatility could also persist if President Trump continues to rely on his executive authority to accomplish his priorities, Yardeni said. In that case, Democrats would have little power to restrain Mr. Trump even if they controlled Congress, he noted.
"Hence, a blue wave could deliver a cold shower for stocks, though we would view a significant selloff as a buying opportunity given the remarkable strength of the economy and corporate earnings," Yardeni said.
A Democratic sweep could have other implications for the economy beyond financial markets. That could include Democrats blocking Trump-appointed regulators, according to Jaret Seiberg, a financial policy analyst and managing director at investment bank TD Cowen.
"They [could] leverage this power to force the President to fill Democratic seats on independent agencies like the FDIC, SEC and CFTC," he said.
A Democratic majority in the Senate would also elevate Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat from Massachusetts, to head the Senate Banking Committee, giving her more latitude to pass populist legislation, Seiberg added. Warren would replace South Carolina Republican Sen. Tim Scott, who currently chairs the influential panel.
However, lawmakers would still be restricted in what they can do at a federal level, given the president's ability to veto legislation, UBS analysts said in a research note.

articles.title_zh: Anthropic is still grappling with the economics of compute
articles.content_orig:
Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

There’s a lot of mystery around the finances of major AI labs, and as Anthropic inches towards it IPO, we’re starting to get some answers. In particular, the company is finally disclosing more about the economics of compute, and how much of Anthropic’s skyrocketing revenue is being lost to compute costs.
In a new filing on Monday , Anthropic released data that showed those margins on compute actually getting worse. The filing was an update to the S-1 released last week — but where that filing’s financial disclosures only covered through June 30 of this year, the new data extended to disclose results through an extra quarter, to September 30. Broadly, Anthropic had a good quarter: revenue reached $17 billion, up from $11.5 billion in the previous quarter, suggesting durable growth. But the operating loss grew at the same time, thanks in large part to growing compute costs.
Looking at the compute margins makes the picture even worse. In the new quarter, compute took up 58% of the company’s revenue, up from 48% the quarter before. At a moment when the company could win over IPO investors by showing margins improving, they’re getting worse.
A chart in the filing shows this even more clearly, tracking the company’s revenue for every dollar spent on compute. Since the start of 2025, it’s been steadily growing, peaking at just over 2x this past quarter, then falling back down to 1.72x.
Many indications imply that this shift in compute margins is more of a blip than a long-term problem, but it still tells us important things about the business of running a major lab. Trying to keep up with demand, Anthropic’s compute bill shot up to $10 billion for the quarter, including, as the filing notes, “$5.0 billion of compute under short-term commitments, which currently costs significantly more than comparable compute procured under our multi-year commitments.” Basically, demand was growing so fast that Anthropic had to scramble for compute, which meant paying higher rates.
Some of those deals have already played out in public. Anthropic has been paying SpaceX $1.25 billion a month for compute, alongside multibillion-dollar deals with Nscale , Akamai , and Volta . In the parlance of the industry, these are neoclouds rather than hyperscalers — smaller outfits that offer more flexible compute deals at higher rates.
Anthropic’s margins got worse in Q3 because of deals like these, and there’s no sign they’ll be able to do without them anytime soon. As the new filing puts it, “We expect compute and infrastructure expenses to increase in absolute dollars and remain our largest operating expense for the foreseeable future as additional committed compute becomes available to us under multi-year arrangements with CSPs, and as we continue to invest in additional compute.”
Anthropic is still trying to lower its compute costs. In particular, the company talks quite a bit about its efforts to build its own compute base under a project it calls “Anthropic Direct.” But with demand growing so fast, those efforts aren’t going to be able to keep pace, and the neoclouds will continue to be the best option they have.
In a sense, these are champagne problems. As long as revenue is growing at nearly 50% a quarter, few investors will worry about high compute costs — and the moment demand slows down, investors may be comforted by a compute picture that has gotten a lot sunnier. But it’s a reminder of how much AI labs still depend on the trillion-dollar infrastructure buildout — and how vulnerable they are to hiccups in that process. It’s easy to imagine the data center buildout slowing down over the next year if bond markets get skittish or local opposition gets more intense. There’s not much Anthropic can do to address either of those risks, and either one would make a messy compute picture a whole lot messier.
In the meantime, the future of Anthropic and other labs will be at the mercy of compute prices.

articles.title_orig: With World of Warcraft: Forever, Blizzard had to reconnect with what made WoW great in the first place
articles.title_zh: With World of Warcraft: Forever, Blizzard had to reconnect with what made WoW great in the first place
articles.content_orig:
A lot of the team had to "unlearn" design habits they picked over the years.
After 13 years at Blizzard, Michael Nuthals faces what might just be the toughest challenge of his career yet: working on a familiar but different and highly anticipated version of World of Warcraft . As lead encounter designer, he's part of the team working on WoW: Forever . Announced at BlizzCon earlier this year, Forever is a sort of remaster of WoW designed to expand on the game's "Classic" era . It takes players back to Azeroth, the setting of the original 2004 game, before Blizzard over the course of 11 expansions took the game in the direction that it did. In the process, it imagines a "what if" scenario.
What if Blizzard had continued to expand Azeroth, instead of sending players to the Orc homeworld of Draenor and beyond with The Burning Crusade and later expansions? In Forever , there are more than 1,000 new quests for players to complete, many of them designed to continue story threads that were left unresolved in the original game. Additionally, there are new areas within Azeroth for players to explore — including Mount Hyjal, the site of one of Warcraft III 's pivotal battles — in addition to fresh dungeons and raids. Blizzard has also rebalanced the game's classes and items, and built an entirely new global illumination lighting pipeline to make the game feel more atmospheric. Controversially, Forever will also feature a new race, the Skyborne Elves, who weren't in the original game.
The challenge Nuthals and his colleagues face is one of expectations. Nearly right from the moment Blizzard rereleased the original World of Warcraft in 2019 , players have been asking the studio for a "Classic+" experience that expands the original game. The tricky thing is that, before Forever's announcement, every player had a different opinion on what an expanded rerelease should look like. Seemingly the only consensus was that the game shouldn't play anything like modern "retail" WoW . Realistically, there was never going to be a way Blizzard would find a way to please everyone with Forever , but it's still trying to create something fans both old and new can appreciate.
"I see it more as an opportunity — an opportunity to engage, to listen and show that we're listening," Nuthals says when asked about the weight of those expectations. With Forever , Blizzard recently concluded the largest beta in World of Warcraft's history . This is despite the fact players had to purchase one of Forever's premium bundles, which start at $60, to take part in the experience. Nuthals says Blizzard received "a lot of feedback" during the beta. He later admits one of the challenges of making Forever has been letting go of habits he learned working on the current version of WoW .
"Some of us had worked on the modern game for a long time, myself included. I come from modern, and it's almost like unlearning what you have learned," said Nuthals, who began working full-time on WoW ahead of 2014's Warlords of Draenor expansion. "We needed to understand what the DNA was [of WoW Classic ], what the philosophies were, and to do that you just had to put it under your fingers and play." One way Nuthals and his colleagues did that was by revisiting the original game each week. Every Thursday morning, he and the rest of the encounter team would replay a classic dungeon like The Deadmines before jumping into one of the new dungeons they've created for Forever , such as Ruins of Lordaeron . Afterwards, they would ask themselves if those two dungeons felt like "they could live hand in glove?" and were connected.
"That was the development process," explains Nuthals. "We thought about what we want Forever to feel like, and we wanted it to feel like you wouldn't even know — like it was made in 2004. That was the vibe we were going for." Nuthals also credits the work Blizzard did with Season of Discovery , which was an offshoot of WoW Classic that saw the studio experiment with new class abilities, progression systems and dungeons within the confines of the original game.
"With Season of Discovery, we were pushing boundaries, exploring what Classic encounters could be. For Forever , we really looked back at the original Classic encounters and wanted to capture those, so we could provide a really authentic and nostalgic experience as players do these new raids," Nuthals said. As part of that process, the one thing he and the team kept coming back to is something Nuthals describes as the "strength, dexterity and intelligence" triangle of encounter design. Strength encounters reward the player for all the gear they've accumulated and their skill with their class, while dexterity ones test how well they can move and avoid hazards. Finally, intelligence-focused encounters test your understanding of a fight's mechanics and how much planning you've done.
"What we're trying to do with raids and dungeons is move toward gearing and planning, because Classic players really love that," said Nuthals. "'I overprepare, then I come in and crush the content.' That was the vibe we really wanted to hit." Part of how that philosophy will play out involves Forever 's much advertised "horizontal" progression. With the new game, the studio has said it plans to keep the level cap at 60, meaning there won't be massive jumps in player power when the studio drops major new content. On paper at least, Blizzard appears committed to rewarding those who engage with and explore the game deeply.
"We're seeding the world with all these new items and things to chase, and in the future, having one of those items might pay off," said Nuthals. "We're thinking about those opportunities as we architect future raids and decide what bosses to introduce: making sure you feel smart for having pocketed something that comes in handy later. It feels good to use all that cool gear you went out and got."
Nuthals also said in the future Blizzard hopes to add new dungeons and zones, and that "not all of them will be max level." He added "there are areas players know about and want to explore, and there are opportunities for us to tell new stories in this space — taking what might have been a one-off quest name or something you found on a piece of paper and developing that story."
One question I didn't get a chance to ask Nuthals is what Blizzard will do if players, upon reaching 60, drop Forever and move onto other games. It's one thing for a studio to say it's committed to doing things differently with an MMO that doesn't take prey on player FOMO, and an entirely different thing to actually stick to that philosophy. We'll see how the future of Forever starts to unfold when the game arrives on November 4 .

articles.title_orig: Death toll rises in Ukraine after Russia attacks aid centre, hospice and hospital
articles.title_zh: Death toll rises in Ukraine after Russia attacks aid centre, hospice and hospital
articles.content_orig:
Other overnight strikes targeted power plants across Ukraine, damaged hospitals and wounded scores of people
Russia has bombed a humanitarian hub in southern Ukraine , killing at least 31 people and leaving dozens missing, as part of a wave of strikes across the country.
Other overnight Russian strikes targeted power plants across Ukraine, damaged hospitals and wounded scores of people, as the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, warned that the US was distracted by its midterm elections.
In total, Russia had launched 289 attack drones, 17 ballistic missiles and 59 cruise missiles across nine regions, triggering emergency power cuts, Zelenskyy said in an online post.
“The Russians think America won’t notice this signal of theirs,” he said. “But we need to notice and stop such terror. We need to help Ukraine defend its skies; otherwise, Russia will never stop its missile strikes,” he said.
The barrage came just a day after a rare local ceasefire in neighbouring Kherson ended, underscoring the limits of the temporary truce.
The deadliest guided-bomb attack first targeted a school building used to distribute humanitarian aid in Komyshuvakha, a village in Ukraine’s southern Zaporizhzhia region, and then took aim at a nearby shelter.
The dead included four police officers and two rescue workers, Mykhailo Semikin, the acting head of the regional military administration, said on Tuesday. At least five people were hurt. Semikin said 48 people were considered missing.
As night fell in Komyshuvakha, emergency responders used torches to search through the rubble of collapsed buildings, according to photos and video posted online by local officials.
Efforts to rescue people on Monday evening were hindered as Russian drones launched additional attacks in the area that had been bombed, according to Mykhailo Semikin, a military official in Zaporizhzhia.
Zelenskyy said the Russians could not have been unaware that residents remaining in Komyshuvakha gathered each week to pick up humanitarian packages from the site.
The attack, he said, had shown that Moscow was intent on killing people instead of building on the past week’s ceasefire in the embattled southern city of Oleshky , brokered by the US first lady, Melania Trump.
“Russians continue to demonstrate, time and again, their hatred of Ukraine and everything that exists here,” Zelenskyy said.
In the north-east region of Kharkiv, a combined Russian missile and drone attack had wounded at least 62 people, local authorities said. A strike damaged a medical facility in the Nemyshlianskyi district, shattered windows in four apartment buildings and damaged cars. More than 200 patients had been transferred to other medical facilities, said the head of the regional military administration, Oleh Syniehubov.
“If Russia genuinely ‌wanted de-escalation, there was an opportunity following the situation in Oleshky to continue taking humanitarian steps. We proposed this. But Russia continues to kill people,” Zelenskyy said.
The ceasefire last week enabled an evacuation of the Russian-occupied Oleshky. It was the longest pause in fighting between the neighbours in the war, now in its fifth year, which has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions.
The Kremlin said that no other similar missions were being planned “at the moment”.
US-led talks between Russia and Ukraine were due to resume next week, the US special envoy Steve Witkoff said on Monday.
Donald Trump, who pledged during his election campaign to end the war in a single day, has repeatedly pushed for a settlement but has so far failed to secure a breakthrough.
The latest round of talks is scheduled for 10-11 November in Abu Dhabi, according to Witkoff, amid growing concerns in Kyiv and among its European allies over Trump’s increasingly close ties with Moscow and discussions of potential business deals between the US and Russia.
Russia announced on Tuesday that its delegation would be led by Vladimir Medinsky, a hardline former culture minister who has headed several previous rounds of negotiations with Ukraine.
Medinsky’s earlier appointment as chief negotiator was met with scepticism by Ukrainian officials and analysts, who questioned whether he had the authority to make meaningful concessions. A key architect of the historical revisionism used by Putin to justify his invasion of Ukraine, Medinsky has long promoted the Kremlin’s narrative that Ukraine is inseparable from Russia.
Zelenskyy, meanwhile, arrived in Berlin for talks with the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz. Germany has become Ukraine’s largest provider of military aid since Merz took office in May 2025, overtaking the US as American support has declined.
The Ukrainian president is also expected to attend this year’s Berlin Security Conference.
Reuters and Agence France-Presse contributed to this report
